pageInfo.subtitle: Master pick-grip physics, edge-picking angles, inside/outside string crossing, and effortless tremolo bursts.
pageInfo.heroDescription: Your picking hand is the motor engine of your guitar playing—it governs rhythmic timing, articulation, dynamic attack, and maximum speed. Before diving into complex solos or intricate rhythm tracks, your picking hand requires systematic calibration. From micro-adjusting pick depth and edge angles to mastering the biomechanical difference between 'inside' and 'outside' string crossing, this warmup routine primes your right wrist and forearm for fluid, relaxed velocity without tension or string snags.

items.text: The Index-Thumb Fulcrum: Clamp the pick securely between the fleshy pad of your thumb and the side of your curled index finger's distal joint, exposing only 2–3 millimeters of the tip.
Edge Picking Angle: Tilt the pick 20 to 30 degrees relative to the string plane so the edge slices across the metal rather than slapping flat, eliminating drag and string click.
Minimal Pick Depth: Submerge only the very tip of the pick past the string boundary; digging deep between the strings creates massive mechanical resistance and caps your speed.
Wrist-Driven Oscillation: Initiate picking strokes primarily from rotational wrist deviation (dart-throwing motion) rather than stiff elbow pumping.
Dynamic Grip Pressure: Hold the pick firm enough to prevent shifting, but relaxed enough that a gentle nudge could pull it from your fingers; tense grips paralyze forearm tendons.

Outside Picking Trajectory: When crossing from a lower string to a higher string, striking with a downstroke on the lower and an upstroke on the higher allows the pick to move outside the string pair.
Inside Picking Calibration: Striking with an upstroke on the lower string and a downstroke on the higher traps the pick between strings, requiring precise micro-escapes.
Continuous Rhythmic Subdivision: Count out 16th notes ('1-e-and-a, 2-e-and-a') in unison with every pick cycle so your hand stays locked to the internal pulse.
Palm Heel Reference Anchor: Rest the fleshy edge of your picking palm lightly on the bass saddles to stabilize your spatial reference without choking string vibration.
Progressive Speed Bursts: Alternate 4 bars of relaxed, slow 8th notes with 2 bars of explosive 16th-note tremolo bursts to train neuromuscular twitch reflexes safely.

sections.title: Foundation: Single-String Speed & Adjacent String Crossing

exercises.title: Single-String Alternate Picking Calibration
exercises.description: Establish absolute right-hand symmetry on a single string. Play strict 16th-note down-up alternate strokes on fret 5 of the G string, focusing on identical volume and transient attack between downstrokes and upstrokes.

patternNote.text: Focus: Symmetrical down/up stroke velocity and minimal pick displacement

practiceNotes.title: Practice Notes
practiceNotes.text: Use a 20-degree edge picking angle. Listen closely: does the upstroke sound as crisp and full as the downstroke? If not, adjust your pick slant until both strokes sound indistinguishable.

exercises.title: Outside Picking Across Adjacent Strings (Strings 4 & 3)
exercises.description: Outside picking occurs when the pick strokes wrap around the outside of two adjacent strings: Downstroke on string 4, Upstroke on string 3. This is the natural and most accessible string-crossing motion.

patternNote.text: Pattern: Downstroke on lower string (4) -> Upstroke on higher string (3)

practiceNotes.title: Practice Notes
practiceNotes.text: Maintain strict down-up alternation throughout. Notice how the pick moves away from the string pair on each stroke, giving maximum clearance.

exercises.title: Inside Picking Across Adjacent Strings (Strings 4 & 3)
exercises.description: Reverse the stroke direction: Upstroke on string 4, Downstroke on string 3. The pick is now trapped inside the string channel, requiring micro-clearing wrist trajectories to avoid snagging.

patternNote.text: Pattern: Upstroke on lower string (4) -> Downstroke on higher string (3)

practiceNotes.title: Practice Notes
practiceNotes.text: Most players find inside picking significantly harder than outside picking. Practice this at 70 BPM until your hand feels just as relaxed inside the strings as outside.

exercises.title: Three-String Economy Roll Warmup (Strings 3, 2, 1)
exercises.description: Warm up economy picking transitions: sweep downwards across strings 3, 2, and 1 in one fluid motion, turnaround with an upstroke on the high E, and sweep upwards across strings 1, 2, and 3.

patternNote.text: Mechanic: Down-Down-Down sweep -> Turnaround -> Up-Up-Up sweep

notation.title: Three-String Economy Picking Roll Across Strings 3, 2, 1

practiceNotes.title: Practice Notes
practiceNotes.text: Do not treat the down-strokes as 3 separate picks; push the pick smoothly through all 3 strings like a miniature downward brush stroke. Reverse smoothly on the turnaround.

sections.title: Advanced Fluency: String Leaps & Tremolo Bursts

exercises.title: Two-String Skipping Picking Warmup (Strings 5 & 3, 4 & 2)
exercises.description: Calibrate wide right-hand spatial leaps. Leap over the 4th string to pick strings 5 and 3, then leap over the 3rd string to pick strings 4 and 2. Keeps the picking hand nimble and agile across wide intervals.

patternNote.text: Mechanic: Micro-arc pick clearance leaping over intermediate strings

practiceNotes.title: Practice Notes
practiceNotes.text: The pick must lift slightly away from the body to vault over the idle string without striking it. Keep the palm heel lightly anchored for spatial accuracy.

exercises.title: The Paul Gilbert 6-Note Alternate Picking Loop
exercises.description: Paul Gilbert's iconic alternate picking loop. Play 5 notes on the B string followed by 1 note on the G string, creating a syncopated 6-against-4 polyrhythmic cycle that challenges picking consistency.

patternNote.text: Pattern: 6-note looping sequence crossing strings 2 and 3

practiceNotes.title: Practice Notes
practiceNotes.text: Because it is a 6-note sequence played in 16th notes, the accent shifts across downbeats and upbeats. Maintain strict alternate picking: do not hammer-on or sweep.

exercises.title: Tremolo Picking Bursts with Dynamic Accents
exercises.description: The ultimate test of right-hand stamina and fluid speed. Execute rapid 16th-note tremolo picking while dynamically accenting beats 1, 2, 3, and 4 on the high E string, then shifting up the neck.

patternNote.text: Tremolo: Continuous alternate picking with heavy downbeat accents

notation.title: High-Speed Tremolo Picking Bursts with Accents

practiceNotes.title: Practice Notes
practiceNotes.text: Keep pick depth strictly minimal—barely skim the top of the string. Emphasize the accented note with a slightly broader wrist flick, then immediately relax back into the rapid flutter.

items.title: 3 Mistakes That Kill Your Picking Hand
items: Digging Too Deep: Allowing more than 3mm of pick tip between strings causes the pick to catch violently on the metal windings, destroying speed and creating forearm fatigue.
The 'Claw' Grip Forearm Tensing: Clamping down on the pick until your knuckles turn white. Rigid hands cannot oscillate at speed; your grip must remain supple and shock-absorbing.
Asymmetrical Pick Trajectory: Slicing on the downstroke but hooking flat on the upstroke. Both strokes must maintain identical edge angles to produce consistent volume and timbre.

items.title: Masters of Picking Articulation
items: Al Di Meola: The undisputed king of muted alternate picking; uses heavy palm damping and razor-precise wrist oscillation to articulate machine-gun Latin fusion runs.
Paul Gilbert: Master of outside picking and 6-note string loops; revolutionized modern picking pedagogy by dissecting pick angles, escaping strokes, and metronomic practice.
John McLaughlin: Blazed Indian classical konnakol and jazz-fusion picking at blazing tempos with the Mahavishnu Orchestra using strict alternate picking discipline.
Steve Morse: Dixie Dregs and Deep Purple legend renowned for his unmatched alternate-picking stamina across complex multi-octave arpeggio sequences.

items.title: The 10-Minute Daily Picking Warmup Routine
items: Block 1: Single-String Symmetrical Calibration (3 min) - Cycle Exercise 1 at 80 BPM, focusing on 20-degree edge angle and identical down/up volume.
Block 2: Outside vs. Inside String Crossing (4 min) - Alternate between Exercises 2 and 3 across strings 4 and 3 at 70–75 BPM, ensuring the pick escapes cleanly.
Block 3: Gilbert Loop & Tremolo Bursts (3 min) - Run the 6-note Gilbert pattern and tremolo bursts at 85–110 BPM to ignite fast-twitch forearm reflexes.

gearRecommendations.title: Recommended Gear for Precision Picking Practice

items.product: Dunlop Flow Standard 1.5mm / Dunlop Jazz III XL
items.reason: The beveled edge and rigid gauge minimize pick drag, allowing instantaneous string release during high-speed alternate picking warmups.
Reduces friction between the pick bevel and wound strings, eliminating annoying string scraping and preserving pick tip sharpness.
